lessons.title: Recover from failed statements and transactions
lessons.summary: Default constraint handling undoes the failed statement.
lessons.body:
The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. Examples of writes start from that original data unless a block explicitly groups statements together.

## Statements are atomic

With the default constraint-error handling used here, a failed statement undoes its row changes. SQLite has other conflict policies: `FAIL` can retain earlier row changes from the same statement, and `IGNORE` can skip offending rows. PostgreSQL sequence increments and external side effects are also not undone by a ROLLBACK:

```sql
-- One invalid row rejects both new
-- products.
INSERT INTO products (name, price)
VALUES ('Jug', 12), ('Tray', NULL);
-- NOT NULL constraint failed
```

Jug was valid, but it is not inserted either. The products table still has five rows.

Inside a transaction, the two databases differ after an error:

- **SQLite**, for the default `ABORT` constraint policy used here, undoes the failed statement. Earlier statements in the transaction remain pending, and `COMMIT` keeps them. Other conflict policies and errors can have different effects.
- **PostgreSQL** marks the whole transaction as failed. Every further statement errors with `current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block`, and `COMMIT` acts as a `ROLLBACK`. Use a `SAVEPOINT` if you want to recover from an error and carry on.

Application code that catches a constraint error and carries on within the same transaction works in SQLite but fails in PostgreSQL.

For PostgreSQL, put the part that may fail after a savepoint. If it fails, roll back to that savepoint before continuing. The rollback removes changes made since the savepoint and clears the failed state for that portion of the transaction; earlier work remains pending. A minimal example uses a duplicate primary key in the shop:

```sql
-- Recover before sending more ordinary
-- work.
BEGIN;
SAVEPOINT optional_insert;
-- Duplicate product 1: expected error.
INSERT INTO products (id, name, price)
VALUES (1, 'Duplicate', 1);
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT optional_insert;
-- The transaction can now read again.
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products;
-- 5: the rejected insert changed no rows
COMMIT;
```

In application code the error handler must actually send the rollback-to-savepoint command. Merely catching the driver exception does not repair PostgreSQL's transaction state. Do not commit earlier work by accident in SQLite either: choose whether the business operation should survive as a whole, and explicitly roll back the whole transaction if it should not.

## Key takeaways
- Default constraint handling undoes the failed statement.
- SQLite ABORT leaves earlier successful transaction statements pending.
- PostgreSQL needs rollback or rollback to a savepoint before more work.

## Further reading
- [Data manipulation — PostgreSQL documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/dml.html)
- [Constraints — PostgreSQL documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html)

questions.prompt:
The products table has 5 rows and `price` is NOT NULL. After running this, how many rows does it have?

```sql
INSERT INTO products (name, price)
VALUES ('Jug', 12),
       ('Tray', NULL);
```

options.explanation: Tray violates NOT NULL, so it can't be inserted. And the error affects the whole statement.

options.text: 6, because Jug is inserted and Tray is rejected
options.explanation: Under the ordinary INSERT behaviour here, a NOT NULL failure undoes every row inserted by this statement, including Jug. SQLite's explicit alternative conflict policies can behave differently.
Correct. Tray's NULL price makes this ordinary INSERT fail and undo its row changes, including Jug. PostgreSQL's consumed sequence values are a separate effect and need not be restored.

options.text: 6, because Tray gets a default price of 0
options.explanation: There's no DEFAULT on price, and an explicit NULL is not "omitted": it is a NULL, which NOT NULL rejects.

questions.workedExample:
1. The statement tries to insert two rows.
2. Tray's price is NULL, so `NOT NULL constraint failed: products.price`.
3. A statement is all-or-nothing, so Jug's insert is undone too.
4. `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products` still returns 5.
5. Note that an explicit `NULL` doesn't bring in a column's DEFAULT; leaving the column out requests the default. PostgreSQL also permits DEFAULT in individual VALUES positions; SQLite instead supports DEFAULT VALUES for a whole default row.

questions.prompt:
In PostgreSQL, a signup handler runs in one transaction:

```
BEGIN
INSERT user (email = dup)  -> error
  (caught: "email taken")
INSERT audit_log (...)
COMMIT
```

The audit insert fails with `current transaction is aborted`. The same code worked on SQLite. Why, and what's a fix?

options.text: The audit table has a foreign key to users
options.explanation: The audit insert isn't rejected for its own content. Every statement fails in an aborted transaction.

options.text: PostgreSQL rolls back only the failed statement, just like SQLite
options.explanation: That's SQLite's behaviour. PostgreSQL marks the whole transaction failed after any error.

options.text: PostgreSQL needs COMMIT before each INSERT
options.explanation: You can run many inserts in one transaction. The error state is what blocks them.

options.text: After an error, PostgreSQL rejects ordinary work until a full rollback or rollback to a savepoint; wrap the risky insert in a SAVEPOINT and roll back to it on error
options.explanation: Correct. `SAVEPOINT s; INSERT ...; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s;` undoes only the failed insert and leaves the transaction usable. `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` avoids the error altogether.

lessons.title: Model relationships and preserve sale prices
lessons.summary: Use a foreign key for one-to-many and a junction table for many-to-many.
lessons.body:
The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. 

Queries come and go, but a schema lasts for years. A badly chosen type or key turns into thousands of lines of defensive code and a data-cleaning project. This lesson is about writing **DDL** (data definition language): `CREATE`, `ALTER` and `DROP`. It also covers the decisions behind those statements.

We'll redesign the module's shop schema from its requirements, then look at how to change it once it's live. Normalisation theory gets its own module (Relational Theory). How tables and indexes are stored on disk is covered in System Design.

## From requirements to tables

The shop's requirements, stated plainly:

- A customer has a name, an optional city, and may have been referred by another customer.
- A product has a name, a price and an optional category.
- A customer places many orders. A guest can also order with no account.
- An order contains many products, each with a quantity, and a product appears in many orders.

Each noun that has its own facts becomes a table. Each relationship becomes a foreign key:

```
customers 1 ──< orders 1 ──< order_items
  ^    │                          >──┐
  └────┘ referred_by                 │
              products 1 ────────────┘
```

| relationship | how it's stored |
|---|---|
| one-to-many | FK on the "many" side |
| many-to-many | a junction table |
| self-reference | FK to the same table |
| optional link | nullable FK |

`orders.customer_id` is the one-to-many link, and it is nullable for guests. `order_items` is the **junction table** that resolves orders-to-products many-to-many. Its primary key is the pair `(order_id, product_id)`: a **composite key**. It also enforces a business rule, because adding a second Kettle to order 101 fails with `UNIQUE constraint failed`. You increase `qty` instead.

### A flaw in our schema

The module's `order_items` stores only a quantity, so an order's total is computed from `products.price` **today**. Raise the Kettle's price and every historical order containing a Kettle changes value. That's wrong for invoices, refunds and accounting.

The fix is to copy the price at the moment of sale into the line item (`unit_pence`). This looks like duplication, but it's a different fact: "what this customer paid" rather than "what the product costs now". Many apparent duplicates in a well-designed schema are really **snapshots** like this.

## Key takeaways
- Use a foreign key for one-to-many and a junction table for many-to-many.
- A composite line key makes each order/product pair unique.
- The sale price is a historical fact distinct from the current product price.

## Further reading
- [Data definition — PostgreSQL documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl.html)

questions.prompt: An order can contain many products and a product can appear in many orders. How should this be modelled?

options.text: Add a `product_ids` text column to orders holding '1,3,5'
options.explanation: A comma-separated list cannot give each member its own ordinary foreign key or quantity. Reading individual ids needs splitting the text. Use separate rows so each order/product association is one value at the intended modelling granularity.
That allows each product to belong to only one order, which is one-to-many in the wrong direction.

options.text: A junction table such as `order_items(order_id, product_id, qty)` with foreign keys to both tables
options.explanation: Correct. Each row links one order to one product and can carry facts about that pairing, such as quantity and price paid.
Repeating columns impose an arbitrary limit, waste space and make "which orders contain a Lamp?" check every column.

questions.workedExample:
1. Many-to-many can't be stored with a single foreign key on either side.
2. Introduce a table whose rows are the pairings:

```sql
-- One row per order and product pair.
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id INTEGER NOT NULL
    REFERENCES orders(id),
  product_id INTEGER NOT NULL
    REFERENCES products(id),
  qty INTEGER NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id,
               product_id));
```

3. The composite primary key stops the same product appearing twice in one order.

questions.prompt: In the module's schema, an order's total is computed as `SUM(order_items.qty * products.price)`. The Kettle's price rises from £30 to £35. What happens to order 101 (one Kettle, four Mugs), placed in January?

options.text: Nothing; past orders are protected by the foreign key
options.explanation: A foreign key only checks that the product exists. It doesn't freeze the product's price.

options.text: Its total changes from £62 to £67, so historical invoices are now wrong; fix it by storing the unit price on each order line
options.explanation: Correct. The total depends on today's price. Copying the price at the time of sale into `order_items` records what the customer actually paid.

options.text: The update fails because orders reference the product
options.explanation: This foreign key references the product ID, so changing price does not violate it. Other constraints or triggers could still reject a price update.

options.text: Its total changes, and that's correct because prices are normalised
options.explanation: Normalisation avoids storing the same fact twice. "Price paid in January" and "current price" are different facts, so storing both isn't duplication.

questions.workedExample:
1. Total the order's lines at today's prices:

```formula
T = Σ (q_i p_i)
T_before = 1 × 30 + 4 × 8 = £62
T_after = 1 × 35 + 4 × 8 = £67
where
T: the order total, in pounds (£)
Σ: the sum over every line i of the order
i: one order line
q_i: the quantity on line i
p_i: line i's current product price (£)
T_before: order 101 before the change
T_after: order 101 after the change
In words: the total is recomputed from today's prices, so a price rise changes old orders.
```

2. The January invoice has changed from £62 to £67.
3. The schema confuses two facts: what a product costs now, and what a customer paid then.
4. Fix: add `unit_pence` to `order_items`, filled from `products` at checkout, and compute totals from it.
5. Many "duplicates" in good schemas are snapshots like this: shipping addresses, tax rates, exchange rates.

lessons.title: Store money without binary rounding errors
lessons.summary: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly.
lessons.body:
The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. 

## Choosing types

### Money: never floating point

```sql
-- SQLite: binary literals expose rounding.
-- SQLite: literals use binary floats.
SELECT 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3;  -- 0 (false)
SELECT 0.1 + 0.2;
-- 0.30000000000000004
```

In PostgreSQL, those uncast decimal literals are exact `numeric` values, so the equality above is TRUE. To demonstrate binary floating point there, cast the operands explicitly:

```sql
-- PostgreSQL: force binary floating point.
-- PostgreSQL: force binary double values.
SELECT 0.1::double precision
     + 0.2::double precision
     = 0.3::double precision;
-- false: the rounded sum differs
```

Binary floating point can't represent most decimal fractions exactly. The reason is in how a floating-point number is built: it is a whole number scaled by an integer power of two.

```formula
x = m 2^e
0.1 = 1 / 10 = 1 / (2 × 5)
where
x: a finite value representable by this binary floating-point form; infinities and NaN are separate special values
m: an integer significand; its magnitude needs at most 53 bits for a binary64 value, up to about 9 × 10^15
e: an integer exponent within the format's range; negative values divide rather than multiply (2^−3 = 1/8)
2^e: e copies of two multiplied together; a negative e means dividing by two that many times
In words: a float can only store fractions whose denominator (the number below the line) is an integer power of two, such as 1/2, 3/8 or 5/1024. A tenth has a factor of 5 below the line, so no choice of m and e gives exactly 0.1, and the nearest storable value is used instead.
```

The stored 0.1 and 0.2 are each a tiny bit off, and their sum lands next to, not on, the stored 0.3. Those small errors build up in sums. Store money either as:

- **integer minor units** (pence): `price_pence INTEGER`, where £10.99 is 1099. This is exact, fast and portable, and it's how payment processors such as Stripe represent amounts.
- **exact decimals**: PostgreSQL `numeric(10,2)`. This is exact, and `SUM` of it stays exact.

Converting between pounds and pence is a single multiplication, done once, when the application reads a price typed by a person or displays one:

```formula
P = 100L
P = 100 × 10.99 = 1099
where
P: the amount in pence, a whole number, which is what is stored in the column
L: the amount in pounds (£), as a person reads it
100: the number of pence in one pound
In words: store the amount as a count of the smallest unit, so every sum and comparison works on exact whole numbers.
```

Parse typed amounts as exact decimals or split the decimal digits into whole pence before storing them. Multiplying an already rounded binary float by 100 can carry a rounding error into the conversion. A fixed-scale numeric column also rounds inputs with extra decimal places, so choose and apply a rounding rule.

Three £10.99 items then sum to 1099 + 1099 + 1099 = 3297 pence, exactly £32.97, with no rounding at any step.

Avoid `real`, `float` and `double precision` for money. Also avoid PostgreSQL's `money` type, whose formatting depends on a server locale setting.

## Key takeaways
- Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly.
- Store money in integer minor units or exact numeric values.
- PostgreSQL uncast decimal literals are numeric, unlike SQLite floating-point literals.

## Further reading
- [Data definition — PostgreSQL documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl.html)
- [Don't do this — PostgreSQL wiki](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This)

questions.prompt: A SQLite developer stores prices in a `REAL` (floating-point) column. A basket check runs `SELECT 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3;` and gets 0 (false). What is the best schema fix?

options.text: Round every result to 2 decimal places in the application
options.explanation: Rounding hides the symptom in one place, but errors still build up in sums, and every query has to remember to round.

options.text: Store amounts as integer pence (or PostgreSQL `numeric`)
options.explanation: Correct. Integers and decimal `numeric` represent amounts exactly, so 10 + 20 = 30 pence with no rounding error. Payment processors such as Stripe use integer minor units.
More bits make the error smaller, not zero: 0.1 has no exact binary representation at any precision.
Its formatting and input depend on the server's locale setting, and the PostgreSQL wiki advises against it. `numeric` or integer pence is safer.

questions.workedExample:
1. 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary floating-point form. Their sum is 0.30000000000000004.
2. That isn't equal to 0.3, so the comparison is false, and long sums drift.
3. Integer pence:

```formula
P = 100L
P = 100 × 10.99 = 1099
3 × P = 3 × 1099 = 3297
where
P: the price in pence, a whole number
L: the price in pounds (£)
100: pence in one pound
In words: in pence every sum is whole-number arithmetic, so three £10.99 items are exactly 3297 pence, £32.97.
```
4. In PostgreSQL, `numeric(10,2)` is an exact decimal alternative.

lessons.title: Represent dates and instants consistently
lessons.summary: PostgreSQL date stores calendar dates; timestamptz stores instants.
lessons.body:
Choosing a column type also determines how dates, instants and text will compare. The shop started with zero-padded ordered_on text; these examples distinguish SQLite representations from PostgreSQL's dedicated types.

### Dates and times

PostgreSQL has real types. Use `date` for calendar dates and `timestamptz` (timestamp with time zone) for moments in time. `timestamptz` stores an absolute instant, internally in UTC, and converts to the session's time zone on display. Plain `timestamp` stores a wall-clock reading with no zone, which becomes ambiguous the moment two servers or users disagree on time zone or a daylight-saving clock change happens. PostgreSQL's own wiki says to prefer `timestamptz`.

SQLite has no date type. Store ISO-8601 text (`'2026-03-09'`, or `'2026-03-09T14:30:00Z'` in UTC). It only sorts correctly if every value uses the same zero-padded format:

```sql
-- Mixed padding breaks chronological
-- sorting.
-- '2026-3-9' vs '2026-03-10'
CREATE TABLE dt (t TEXT);
INSERT INTO dt VALUES
  ('2026-3-9'), ('2026-03-10');
SELECT t FROM dt ORDER BY t;
-- 2026-03-10
-- 2026-3-9    (wrong!)
```

A CHECK can reject badly formatted values at write time, but beware the NULL lesson. SQLite's `date('2026-3-9')` returns NULL, so `CHECK (d = date(d))` is UNKNOWN and **passes**. Use the NULL-safe form:

```sql
-- SQLite column definition in CREATE TABLE.
d TEXT NOT NULL
  CHECK (d IS date(d))
```

This rejects `'2026-3-9'`, and also `'2026-02-30'`, which `date()` turns into `'2026-03-02'`.

### Text

In PostgreSQL, `text` and `varchar(n)` are stored the same way and perform the same. `varchar(n)` just adds a length check. Use `text`, and add a `CHECK (length(name) <= 200)` where a limit is a real business rule. Avoid `char(n)`, which pads with spaces.

## Key takeaways
- PostgreSQL date stores calendar dates; timestamptz stores instants.
- Consistent zero-padded UTC text sorts correctly in SQLite.
- Use a NULL-safe date check to reject unparseable input.

## Further reading
- [Data definition — PostgreSQL documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl.html)
- [Don't do this — PostgreSQL wiki](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This)

questions.prompt:
To reject badly formatted dates in SQLite, a developer writes:

```sql
d TEXT CHECK (d = date(d))
```

`INSERT ... VALUES ('2026-3-9')` succeeds. Why?

options.text: SQLite ignores CHECK constraints unless a pragma is on
options.explanation: CHECK constraints are enabled by default. They can be disabled with `PRAGMA ignore_check_constraints`, but this example succeeds because UNKNOWN satisfies CHECK, not because enforcement was disabled.

options.text: `date('2026-3-9')` returns NULL, so the CHECK is UNKNOWN, and a CHECK only fails on FALSE
options.explanation: Correct. SQLite's `date()` returns NULL for input it can't parse. `d = NULL` is UNKNOWN, which passes. Use `CHECK (d IS date(d))` instead.

options.text: `date()` normalises '2026-3-9' to '2026-03-09', which equals the input
options.explanation: If it returned '2026-03-09', the comparison would be FALSE (the strings differ) and the insert would fail. It actually returns NULL.

options.text: Text can't be compared with a date in SQLite
options.explanation: SQLite has no date type; `date()` returns text, so it's a plain text comparison.

questions.workedExample:
1. `date('2026-3-9')` → NULL, because it's not a format SQLite recognises.
2. The check becomes `'2026-3-9' = NULL` → UNKNOWN.
3. CHECK rejects only FALSE, so the row is accepted.
4. Fix with the NULL-safe comparison:

```sql
-- Column inside CREATE TABLE dates.
d TEXT NOT NULL
  CHECK (d IS date(d))
```

Now '2026-3-9' fails (text IS NULL is false), and '2026-02-30' fails too, because `date()` turns it into '2026-03-02'.

lessons.title: Enforce types and separate identity from business keys
lessons.summary: Ordinary SQLite type affinity can store text in an INTEGER column.
lessons.body:
The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. 

## SQLite's type affinity versus strict typing

PostgreSQL rejects a value of the wrong type. SQLite, by default, treats the declared type as a preference, called **type affinity**:

```sql
-- Affinity converts values when possible.
CREATE TABLE loose
  (n INTEGER, d TEXT);
INSERT INTO loose VALUES
  ('abc', 12), ('42', 3.5);
```

| n | typeof(n) | d | typeof(d) |
|---|---|---|---|
| abc | text | 12 | text |
| 42 | integer | 3.5 | text |

`'42'` was converted to an integer because it looked like one. `'abc'` couldn't be converted, so SQLite stored text in an INTEGER column without complaint. Since 3.37, a `STRICT` table rejects incompatible stored values, although its supported type names and conversion rules still differ from PostgreSQL:

```sql
-- STRICT refuses the incompatible value.
CREATE TABLE tight
  (n INTEGER, d TEXT) STRICT;
INSERT INTO tight VALUES ('abc', 'x');
-- cannot store TEXT value in
-- INTEGER column tight.n
```

`'42'` is still converted to 42, which is a lossless change. Use `STRICT` for new SQLite tables.

## Keys

A **natural key** is a real-world identifier: an email address, an ISBN, a vehicle registration. A **surrogate primary key** is a meaningless generated number or UUID.

Natural keys look attractive, but real-world identifiers change (people change email; registrations are transferred) and are rarely as unique as promised. A primary key is copied into every referencing table, so changing it means updating them all. The common pattern is:

- a surrogate primary key for identity and foreign keys, and
- a `UNIQUE` constraint on the natural key to enforce the business rule.

```sql
-- Column definition inside CREATE TABLE.
email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
```

Watch case: `'Asha@x.com'` and `'asha@x.com'` are different strings, so both pass a plain UNIQUE. A unique index on `lower(email)` catches it (PostgreSQL also offers the `citext` extension).

## Key takeaways
- Ordinary SQLite type affinity can store text in an INTEGER column.
- STRICT tables require compatible values, including lossless conversions.
- Keep mutable business identifiers UNIQUE beside a stable surrogate primary key.

## Further reading
- [Datatypes in SQLite (type affinity)](https://www.sqlite.org/datatype3.html)
- [STRICT tables — SQLite documentation](https://www.sqlite.org/stricttables.html)

SQLite doesn't invent a number. It converts only text that looks like a number.
The value isn't discarded; it is stored as given.
Correct. INTEGER affinity converts text only when it looks like a number. `'abc'` doesn't, so it is stored as text in an INTEGER column.

questions.prompt: A team proposes making `email` the primary key of `customers`, since emails are unique. Orders and five other tables would reference it. What's the main problem?

options.text: Text primary keys aren't allowed in PostgreSQL

options.text: Emails are too long to index

options.explanation: Correct. A primary key is copied into every foreign key. Natural identifiers change, so a stable surrogate primary key plus a UNIQUE constraint gives you both identity and the business rule.
That's a point in email's favour as a key. The trouble is that it changes, not that it's missing.

1. A primary key's job is to identify a row stably for its whole life.
2. Emails change (new job, new provider), and sometimes need merging or correcting.
3. With email as the PK, a change means updating orders and every other referencing table, or relying on `ON UPDATE CASCADE` across large tables.
4. Pattern:

```sql
-- Columns inside CREATE TABLE

```

lessons.title: Generate ids without collisions or unwanted reuse
lessons.summary: Identity sequences do not advance when an explicit id bypasses generation.
lessons.body:
The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. 

### Generating ids

| database | declaration |
|---|---|
| PostgreSQL 10+ | `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` |
| PostgreSQL (older) | `serial` / `bigserial` |
| SQLite | `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` |

In PostgreSQL, prefer identity columns to `serial`. They are standard SQL, and `ALWAYS` rejects hand-written ids unless the insert says `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`. That matters because inserting explicit ids into a `serial` or `BY DEFAULT` column doesn't advance the sequence, and a later generated id collides with `duplicate key value violates unique constraint`. Use `bigint` for ids of any table that might grow large. A signed integer column spends one bit on the sign, so its largest value is:

```formula
N_max = 2^{b − 1} − 1
N_32 = 2^31 − 1 = 2,147,483,647
N_64 = 2^63 − 1 ≈ 9.2 × 10^18
where
N_max: the largest value a signed integer of b bits can hold
b: the number of bits in the type: 32 for PostgreSQL integer, 64 for bigint
N_32: the limit of a 32-bit integer column, about 2.1 billion
N_64: the limit of a 64-bit bigint column
≈: approximately equal to
In words: each extra bit doubles the range, and one bit is used for the sign, so a 32-bit id runs out after about 2.1 billion values while a 64-bit id effectively never does.
```

Running out of 32-bit ids has caused real outages. At 1,000 new rows a second, 2.1 billion ids last about 2,147,483,647 / 1,000 ≈ 2.1 million seconds, under 25 days; the same rate would take about 290 million years to exhaust a bigint. Gaps from rolled-back inserts use up ids faster than the row count suggests.

In SQLite, an `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` column becomes an alias for the table's internal **rowid**. New ids normally follow a simple rule:

```formula
id_new = max(rowid) + 1
id_new = 4 + 1 = 5
where
id_new: the id SQLite gives the next inserted row when you don't supply one
max: the largest of a set of values
rowid: the ids currently in the table; after deleting product 5, the largest is 4
In words: the next id is one more than the largest id still in the table, so the id of a deleted newest row comes straight back.
```

(An empty table starts at 1.) This ordinary rule assumes the current largest rowid is below the signed 64-bit maximum; at that maximum SQLite tries unused positive ids instead. So deleting the newest row lets its id be **reused**. Delete product 5 and the next insert gets id 5 again. Adding `AUTOINCREMENT` prevents automatic reuse of IDs from previously committed rows, at a small cost. IDs from rolled-back transactions can still be reused, and explicit IDs require separate care. It's only needed when old ids might linger elsewhere, in logs, caches or URLs.

UUIDs make sense when ids are generated outside the database. Random UUIDv4 values can make identifiers difficult to guess, but an id is never a substitute for authorisation. They scatter inserts across a B-tree index. Time-ordered UUIDv7 improves insertion locality, while exposing approximate generation time; PostgreSQL 18 added a built-in `uuidv7()` function.

## Key takeaways
- Identity sequences do not advance when an explicit id bypasses generation.
- Choose an identifier capacity that fits growth and consumed sequence values.
- SQLite normally reuses a deleted highest rowid unless AUTOINCREMENT prevents it.

## Further reading
- [Data definition — PostgreSQL documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl.html)
- [SQLite autoincrement](https://www.sqlite.org/autoinc.html)

questions.prompt: A SQLite table has `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` (no AUTOINCREMENT) and rows with ids 1 to 5. You delete row 5 and insert a new row. What id does it get, and why might that matter?

options.explanation: Without AUTOINCREMENT, SQLite uses the current maximum + 1. After deleting 5, the maximum is 4.

options.text: 1, because SQLite fills the first gap
options.explanation: SQLite doesn't search for gaps; it takes the maximum id + 1.

options.text: 5; anything that still refers to the old product 5 (a URL, a cache, a log) now points at a different row
options.explanation: Correct. The new row reuses the deleted id. AUTOINCREMENT prevents automatic reuse of previously committed rowids, but not reuse after rollback or a deliberately supplied explicit id.

options.text: NULL, because the sequence is broken
options.explanation: An INTEGER PRIMARY KEY can't be NULL; SQLite always assigns a value.

questions.workedExample:
1. `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` normally aliases the rowid in a SQLite rowid table.
2. Here max(rowid) is 5, then becomes 4 after the deletion.
3. The next automatically generated ID is therefore:

```formula
id_new = max(rowid) + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5
where
id_new: the id given to the new row
max: the largest of a set of values
rowid: the ids now in the table (1 to 4)
In words: one more than the largest id still present.
```
4. With `AUTOINCREMENT`, the recorded maximum from committed rows remains 5, so the next automatically generated ID is 6. Rolled-back IDs are not protected from reuse.
5. PostgreSQL sequences normally advance independently of transaction rollback, but explicit resets or CYCLE can reuse values. Enforce row uniqueness with a primary key and do not assume gapless IDs.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL table has `id integer GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY`. A data import inserts rows with explicit ids 1 to 1,000. The next normal insert fails with `duplicate key value violates unique constraint`. Why?

options.text: Identity columns can't accept explicit values
options.explanation: `BY DEFAULT` accepts explicit values. `ALWAYS` would have rejected them unless the insert said `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`.
The imported ids 1 to 1,000 were unique. The clash is between an imported id and a *newly generated* one.

options.text: Explicit ids don't advance the identity's sequence, so it still hands out 1, which already exists; reset it past the imported maximum
options.explanation: Correct. The sequence only moves when it generates a value. After the import, restart it (for example `ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN id RESTART WITH 1001`).
1,000 rows is nowhere near the 32-bit limit of about 2.1 billion. This is a sequence-position problem.

questions.workedExample:
1. An identity column is backed by a sequence that produces the next value only when asked.
2. The import supplied ids 1 to 1,000 itself, so the sequence was never called and is still at its start.
3. The next ordinary insert asks the sequence for a value, gets 1, and collides.
4. Fix after any import with explicit ids:

```sql
-- Generate beyond the imported ids.
ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN id
  RESTART WITH 1001;
```

5. `GENERATED ALWAYS` makes accidental explicit ids an error in the first place, which is why it's the safer default.

lessons.title: Read a constrained PostgreSQL shop schema
lessons.summary: Constrain prices, quantities and statuses in the schema.
lessons.body:
The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. 

## The redesigned schema in PostgreSQL

```sql
-- Run this redesign in an empty database.
CREATE TABLE customers (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS
     AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name text NOT NULL,
  email text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  city text,
  referred_by bigint
    REFERENCES customers (id)
    ON DELETE SET NULL,
  created_at timestamptz
    NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE products (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS
     AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name text NOT NULL,
  price_pence integer NOT NULL
    CHECK (price_pence >= 0),
  category text
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS
     AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id bigint
    REFERENCES customers (id),
  placed_at timestamptz NOT NULL
    DEFAULT now(),
  status text NOT NULL
    DEFAULT 'pending'
    CHECK (status IN ('pending',
      'shipped', 'cancelled'))
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id bigint NOT NULL
    REFERENCES orders (id)
    ON DELETE CASCADE,
  product_id bigint NOT NULL
    REFERENCES products (id),
  qty integer NOT NULL
    CHECK (qty > 0),
  unit_pence integer NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);

CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id);
CREATE INDEX ON order_items
  (product_id);
```

Notice the decisions:

- `orders.customer_id` is nullable (guests) and uses the default `NO ACTION`, so a customer with orders can't be deleted by accident.
- `order_items` cascades: lines don't exist without their order.
- `unit_pence` snapshots the price.
- The `status` list is a CHECK. The alternatives are a PostgreSQL `ENUM` type (compact; values can be renamed with `ALTER TYPE`, but removing one requires a more involved migration) or a `statuses` lookup table with a foreign key (best when statuses carry their own data, or business users add them).

Use lower-case `snake_case` names. PostgreSQL folds unquoted identifiers to lower case, so a table created as `"OrderItems"` must be double-quoted in every query forever.

### Index your foreign keys

Neither PostgreSQL nor SQLite automatically adds a database index merely because a column is **referencing** a foreign key. Both provide indexed enforcement for primary and UNIQUE keys; SQLite's INTEGER PRIMARY KEY uses the rowid structure. Without an index beginning with `customer_id`, finding "orders for customer 1" can require a full table scan. In this SQLite fixture, `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` shows `SCAN orders` before the index and `SEARCH orders USING INDEX` after. A missing FK index can also force scans of the child table when a parent is deleted. `order_items` already has indexed access by `order_id`, the first column of its primary key. Real planners can still choose a scan when a small table makes it cheaper.

## Key takeaways
- Constrain prices, quantities and statuses in the schema.
- Snapshot unit_pence on each order line.
- Add suitable indexes on referencing foreign key columns.

## Further reading
- [Data definition — PostgreSQL documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl.html)
- [Don't do this — PostgreSQL wiki](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This)

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, you create the schema from the lesson **without** any `CREATE INDEX` statements. Which columns are the **first key column** of an automatically created index? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Correct. PostgreSQL creates a unique index to enforce every PRIMARY KEY.
Correct. A UNIQUE constraint is enforced with a unique index, created automatically.
Neither PostgreSQL nor SQLite indexes the referencing column of a foreign key automatically. You must create it, or lookups and parent deletes scan the table.

options.text: `order_items.order_id` (first column of the composite primary key)
options.explanation: Correct. The primary key index on `(order_id, product_id)` can serve lookups by `order_id` alone, because it is the leading column.

It is included in the composite primary-key index, but is its second key column. It is not the first key of an automatically created index. A separate index may help product-only lookups; PostgreSQL can sometimes use a scan or skip scan of the composite index.

questions.workedExample:
1. PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraints create indexes automatically.
2. The indexes begin with customers.id, customers.email and order_items.order_id.
3. orders.customer_id has no automatically created index here.
4. order_items.product_id is the second key in (order_id, product_id), not its leading key. A product-only lookup may scan that index or, with a suitable PostgreSQL version and distribution, use skip scan.
5. Consider a separate product_id index after examining the actual plan.

lessons.title: Evolve SQLite tables within supported ALTER operations
lessons.summary: Migrations apply versioned schema changes in order.
lessons.body:
The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. 

## Changing a live schema

Schemas change for as long as the application lives, through **migrations**: versioned DDL scripts applied in order by tools such as Flyway, Alembic or Rails migrations. Developers can rely on a few rules of thumb.

### What SQLite can ALTER

SQLite has long supported `RENAME TO`, `RENAME COLUMN` (3.25), `ADD COLUMN`, and `DROP COLUMN` (3.35). Version 3.53.0 (April 2026) added `ALTER COLUMN ... SET NOT NULL` and `DROP NOT NULL`, plus adding and dropping named CHECK constraints. Anything else, such as changing a type or adding a foreign key, still means the documented rebuild: create a new table, copy the rows across, drop the old table and rename the new one, all in one transaction.

For a populated table, adding an ordinary `NOT NULL` column needs a non-NULL value for existing rows, commonly supplied by a default. PostgreSQL can add it without a default to an empty table; SQLite imposes its documented default restriction:

```sql
-- Try each addition on a fresh populated
-- shop.
ALTER TABLE customers
  ADD COLUMN phone TEXT NOT NULL;
-- SQLite: Cannot add a NOT NULL
-- column with default value NULL
ALTER TABLE customers
  ADD COLUMN tier TEXT NOT NULL
  DEFAULT 'std';   -- fine
```

For these two alternatives, use separate copies of the original populated customers table. The failed phone addition leaves its schema unchanged. The tier addition succeeds and gives each of its five existing rows the value `std`; later inserts that omit tier receive the same default. A default is used for omission, so it does not turn an explicitly supplied NULL into `std`.

Before a rebuild, inspect the original schema's constraints, indexes, triggers and dependent views. Copying just its column names can silently drop protection or break dependencies. Follow SQLite's documented rebuild sequence, preserve the objects that still apply, and run `PRAGMA foreign_key_check` before committing. If a step fails, explicitly roll back instead of committing the earlier successful steps. Rehearse the migration on a copy and verify both the resulting schema and row counts.

## Key takeaways
- Migrations apply versioned schema changes in order.
- SQLite ALTER support depends on the engine version.
- A new required column needs values for existing rows; a default can provide them.

## Further reading
- [ALTER TABLE — SQLite documentation](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_altertable.html)

questions.prompt: A populated SQLite customers table needs a required tier column. Which addition also gives every existing row a value?

options.explanation: Without a non-NULL default, SQLite cannot supply the required value for the existing rows.

options.text: `ADD COLUMN tier TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'std'`
options.explanation: Correct. The default supplies std for existing rows and for later inserts that omit tier.
SQLite does not permit a UNIQUE column in ADD COLUMN, and uniqueness would not make a value required.
The default remains NULL and there is no NOT NULL requirement, so this does not enforce the intended rule.

questions.workedExample:
1. The existing five customers need a value even though they were inserted before tier existed.
2. A default of std supplies that value.
3. NOT NULL rejects explicitly supplied NULLs; a default alone does not.
4. Run the addition, then inspect the existing rows:

```sql
ALTER TABLE customers
  ADD COLUMN tier TEXT NOT NULL
  DEFAULT 'std';
-- Old rows receive the new default.
SELECT name, tier FROM customers;
```

Each of the five original customers has tier std.

lessons.title: Keep PostgreSQL migration locks short
lessons.summary: Metadata changes can still wait for and hold blocking locks.
lessons.body:
The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. 

### PostgreSQL: watch the locks

Most `ALTER TABLE` forms take an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock, which blocks reads and writes on that table. Whether that matters depends on how long the lock is held:

- **Fast, metadata only:** adding a nullable column, or (since PostgreSQL 11) adding a column with a non-volatile default such as `'std'` or `now()`. This avoids work that grows with the number of rows, but lock waits and catalogue work still determine the elapsed time.
- **Slow, rewrites or scans:** changing a column's type, adding a column with a volatile default such as `clock_timestamp()`, or `SET NOT NULL`, which scans every row to check.

Even a fast `ALTER` can cause an outage. If a long-running query holds a lock on the table, the `ALTER` waits for it, and every new query queues behind the `ALTER`. Set `lock_timeout` (for example `SET lock_timeout = '2s'`) so the migration fails fast and can be retried.

For slow changes, split the work so that the long validation phase permits ordinary reads and writes. The short catalogue changes still take locks:

This migration assumes an existing nullable `customers.email` column whose older rows have already been populated. It upgrades that older schema to require email; the completed redesign in the earlier unit already makes email required.

```sql
-- PostgreSQL: validate existing email
-- values.
-- 1. add, not yet checked
ALTER TABLE customers
  ADD CONSTRAINT email_nn
  CHECK (email IS NOT NULL)
  NOT VALID;
-- 2. validate while ordinary writes run
ALTER TABLE customers
  VALIDATE CONSTRAINT email_nn;
-- 3. PG 12+ uses the valid CHECK
--    to skip the scan
ALTER TABLE customers
  ALTER COLUMN email SET NOT NULL;
```

Indexes follow the same idea. Plain `CREATE INDEX` blocks ordinary writes for the whole build. `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` permits ordinary writes, but requires extra scans and waits, cannot run inside a transaction block, and can leave an `INVALID` index after a failure. Inspect a failed build and normally drop or rebuild the invalid index before retrying.

Renaming or dropping a column that running code still uses breaks that code instantly. The safe pattern is **expand and contract**: add the new column, deploy code that writes both while still reading the old one, and wait until every writer uses that code or a synchronisation trigger covers older writers. Backfill in batches, verify agreement, switch reads, and keep dual writes until every reader has migrated. Only then stop writing and drop the old column in a later release. Switching reads while older writers still update only the original column exposes stale data.

## Key takeaways
- Metadata changes can still wait for and hold blocking locks.
- Use lock_timeout to fail a waiting migration promptly.
- Validate constraints separately and expand-and-contract incompatible column changes.

## Further reading
- [ALTER TABLE — PostgreSQL documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-altertable.html)

questions.prompt: Your PostgreSQL 16 `orders` table has 500 million rows. Which change is a quick metadata-only operation, with no table rewrite or full scan?

options.explanation: Changing a column's type to one with a different storage format rewrites the whole table, holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock throughout.

options.text: `ADD COLUMN channel text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'web'`
options.explanation: Correct. Since PostgreSQL 11, a non-volatile default is stored in the catalogue and returned for old rows, so no rewrite is needed.
`clock_timestamp()` is volatile: each row needs its own value, so PostgreSQL must rewrite the table.
Adding a validated CHECK normally scans the existing rows to prove the rule. It does not rewrite the table, but it is not a scan-free metadata-only addition.

questions.workedExample:
Classify each change:

| change | cost |
|---|---|
| int → bigint | rewrite |
| add, constant default | metadata |
| add, volatile default | rewrite |
| SET NOT NULL | full scan |

2. `clock_timestamp()` differs per row, so every row must be physically written.
3. Even the fast one takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock briefly, so run it with a `lock_timeout`.

questions.prompt: A migration runs `ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text;`, normally an instant change. This time the site goes down for 4 minutes. A reporting query had been reading `orders` for 4 minutes. What happened, and what prevents it?

options.text: The ALTER rewrote the table; use a default value
options.explanation: Adding a nullable column with no default is metadata-only. No rewrite happened.

options.text: The report held a lock, so the ALTER queued for its ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, and every new query on orders queued behind the ALTER; set `lock_timeout` so the migration gives up and retries
options.explanation: Correct. Lock requests queue in order. The waiting ALTER blocks even plain SELECTs that arrive after it. A short `lock_timeout` makes the ALTER fail fast instead of stalling everything.

options.text: ALTER TABLE always blocks for as long as the table is large
options.explanation: The duration depends on the operation and on lock waits, not on table size, for metadata-only changes.

options.text: The report query was blocked by the new column
options.explanation: The report started first and already held its lock. It was everything *after* the ALTER that was blocked.

questions.workedExample:
1. The report holds an ACCESS SHARE lock on `orders` for 4 minutes.
2. The ALTER needs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, which conflicts, so it waits.
3. New queries need ACCESS SHARE. That doesn't conflict with the report, but it does conflict with the *queued* ALTER, so they wait behind it.
4. Result: every query on `orders` stalls until the report finishes.
5. Prevention:

```sql
-- Give up promptly if a lock blocks us.
SET lock_timeout = '2s';
ALTER TABLE orders
  ADD COLUMN note text;
-- retry on failure
```

Also cap long queries with `statement_timeout`.

questions.prompt: You must rename `customers.city` to `town` in PostgreSQL with no downtime, while old and new application versions run side by side during the deploy. Which steps belong in a safe expand-and-contract plan? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Correct. Adding a nullable column is metadata-only and breaks nothing.

options.text: Deploy code that writes to both columns and reads from `city`
options.explanation: Correct. Both old and new versions keep working, and new writes populate `town`.

options.text: Run `ALTER TABLE customers RENAME COLUMN city TO town` in the first deploy
options.explanation: The rename is instant, but every running instance of the old code that still says `city` fails immediately. That's the outage you were trying to avoid.

options.text: Backfill `town` from `city` in small batches, then switch reads to `town`
options.explanation: Correct. Small batches keep row locks and WAL bursts short, and reads switch only once the data is complete.

options.text: Drop `city` in a later release, once no running code uses it
options.explanation: Correct. Contract last, when nothing depends on the old column.

questions.workedExample:
Expand and contract, in order:

1. **Expand**: add nullable `town` (metadata-only, but still lock-sensitive).
2. Deploy code that writes both columns and continues reading `city`. Wait until all writers use it, or use a carefully designed synchronisation trigger for older writers.
3. Backfill in batches while dual writes keep both columns current. Verify that values agree before switching reads.
4. Switch reads to `town` but keep dual writes until every reader has migrated; then stop writing `city`.
5. **Contract**: drop `city` only once no running code uses it.

Switching reads while old writers still update only `city` can expose stale values in `town`. Small batches and lock timeouts control operational impact.

lessons.title: Use stored queries and roll back schema changes
lessons.summary: A normal view stores a query; a materialised view stores its result.
lessons.body:
The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. 

## Views and DROP

A **database view** is a named, stored query:

```sql
-- Save the total calculation as a named
-- query.
CREATE VIEW order_totals AS
SELECT oi.order_id,
  SUM(oi.qty * p.price) AS total
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p
  ON p.id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY oi.order_id;
```

`SELECT * FROM order_totals WHERE total > 60` returns 101 (62), 102 (80) and 104 (70). A view stores no data; it runs its query each time. PostgreSQL's `MATERIALIZED VIEW` stores the result and needs `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW` to update it.

The view inherits the price-history flaw discussed earlier: changing today's product price changes a total recomputed from `products.price`. On the redesigned schema, total the saved `qty * unit_pence` instead. Naming a query does not change which facts it reads or turn a live calculation into a historical snapshot.

Transactional DDL lets you rehearse a small change and undo it. This complete example works in SQLite and PostgreSQL:

```sql
-- Rollback removes the table as well as its
-- row.
BEGIN;
CREATE TABLE migration_probe (n integer);
INSERT INTO migration_probe VALUES (7);
ROLLBACK;
-- The new table and its row are gone.
```

After rollback, selecting from `migration_probe` raises a missing-table error. The original shop tables are unaffected. This guarantee concerns supported transactional operations: PostgreSQL's `CREATE DATABASE` and `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, for example, cannot run inside a transaction block. Check the command's documentation instead of assuming every administrative statement is transactional.

`DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t` tolerates a missing table, so that particular drop can be repeated. It does not make an entire migration safe to repeat. In PostgreSQL, `DROP TABLE t CASCADE` also removes dependent views and foreign key constraints without a separate approval prompt; the referencing tables remain. SQLite and PostgreSQL support transactional DDL for operations such as these. Explicitly roll back a failed migration: PostgreSQL normally aborts the transaction after an error, whereas SQLite can leave earlier successful statements pending and a later COMMIT could retain them. Most MySQL DDL implicitly commits, which is one reason migrations there need extra care.

## Key takeaways
- A normal view stores a query; a materialised view stores its result.
- DROP CASCADE can remove dependent views and constraints.
- Transactional DDL needs explicit transaction error handling; MySQL most DDL implicitly commits.

## Further reading
- [Data definition — PostgreSQL documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl.html)
- [ALTER TABLE — PostgreSQL documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-altertable.html)

options.explanation: ROLLBACK undoes the insert and the table creation in both engines.

options.text: An empty result from an existing table
options.explanation: The CREATE TABLE is transactional too, so the table itself does not remain.
Correct. Rolling back this supported transactional DDL removes the table created inside the transaction.
The new table has a separate name and never referred to products; rollback leaves the shop untouched.

2. CREATE TABLE and INSERT belong to it.
3. ROLLBACK undoes both, so the name migration_probe no longer exists.
4. A subsequent SELECT raises a missing-table error. This applies to these commands in SQLite and PostgreSQL; it is not a promise about every engine or administrative command.
